title: Binary to Gray Code
statement:
Convert a 4-bit binary value into its 4-bit reflected Gray code.

## Your entity

```
entity solution is
    port (
        bin  : in  std_logic_vector(3 downto 0);
        gray : out std_logic_vector(3 downto 0)
    );
end entity solution;
```

Gray code is the encoding used on rotary encoders and grey-scale counters:
adjacent values -- `n` and `n+1` -- differ in exactly one bit, which is what
makes it safe to *sample* mid-transition (an ordinary binary counter can be
briefly misread as anything, because several bits can be changing at once;
a Gray-coded one is misread as its neighbour at worst).

`"1010"` (decimal 10) becomes `"1111"`. `"0111"` (decimal 7) becomes
`"0100"`.

## Input and output

The testbench reads one line of stdin as a 4-character bit string, drives
it onto `bin`, waits for the output to settle, and writes `gray` back out
the same way.

## Watch out

- The top bit is unchanged: `gray(3) = bin(3)`. Every other output bit is
  the XOR of the binary input bit at its own position *and the position one
  above it* -- `gray(i) = bin(i+1) xor bin(i)` for `i` from 2 downto 0.
  Getting that shift backwards (`bin(i) xor bin(i-1)`, say) still produces
  *a* 4-bit output for every input, so nothing about it fails to compile --
  it is simply the wrong 4 bits for every input except zero.

tests.name: zero
tests.description: Binary and Gray agree at zero.

tests.name: ten
tests.description: Every output bit differs from the input, which is as far from a lookup-table shortcut as a 4-bit case gets.

tests.name: all ones
tests.description: The top bit passes straight through even when every input bit is set.
